decision: Skenes's 67.5 ERA after two-thirds of an inning says almost nothing; the denominator will make it fade over coming starts.
original_tool: denominator sensitivity arithmetic, Bayesian Gamma-Poisson recovery
anova_analysis: none possible (one start; at most this start vs career starts, n=1)
why: The tool has no way to state how long a rate on a tiny denominator takes to normalize.

decision: No mock draft can be perfect, yet the best analysts beat chance by a wide margin (about 12 matches vs about 1).
anova_analysis: one-sample t-test of analysts' exact-match counts against an assumed chance mean
why: The headline is the chance of a perfect mock, and the chance baseline itself needs combinatorics the analyst lacks.

decision: The transfer order cuts portal moves by about a third; HS-first programs gain and portal-built programs lose.
original_tool: scenario projection arithmetic, descriptive program table
anova_analysis: t-test of net portal flow, HS-first vs portal-dependent programs (5 vs 4)
why: The decision is a projected effect of a new rule, which no group comparison of past data can produce.

decision: The Rangers are collapsing, the Sabres rising and Vegas aging; youth, patience and draft capital mark the trajectory.
original_tool: descriptive point-percentage trends, qualitative factor table
anova_analysis: one-way ANOVA of point percentage by season within each club (n=3 seasons)
why: The issue's trajectory reading is descriptive with no inference, so the analyst would read the same trends.

decision: WNBA and MLS salaries are within 8%; the real gap is the share of revenue WNBA players capture.
anova_analysis: two-sample t-test of player salaries, WNBA vs MLS
why: A skewed-salary t-test would likely call the 8% gap 'no difference' and miss the revenue-share point entirely.

decision: Jets and Giants first-round drafting is comparable; the Giants' edge came from elsewhere.
original_tool: descriptive bust rates under three definitions
anova_analysis: t-test of first-round bust indicator, Jets vs Giants picks
why: The analyst reaches 'comparable' by p > .05 on binary busts, reading a non-significant 71% vs 56% gap as no difference.

decision: A coach's or pick's ceiling shows by years 2-3; teams wait too long.
original_tool: correlation of year-N record with career record (cited/approximate)
anova_analysis: median split coaches on year-2 win%, t-test of career win% between halves, repeated per year
why: Split t-tests would all be significant and point to 'judge early', but cannot show where the information curve flattens.

decision: One season reveals about 60% of a coach's true ability and three seasons about 82%; five-year patience is mostly wasted.
anova_analysis: median split on year-1 win%, t-test of later win%
why: A significant split says early record matters, the same direction, but loses the 60%/82% stabilization curve that is the point.

decision: Teams differ far more on late-round drafting than early-round; the two rankings tell different stories.
original_tool: hit rates by team, coefficient of variation comparison
anova_analysis: one-way ANOVA of hit (0/1) by team, separately for rounds 1-3 and 4-7
why: Early-round ANOVA would likely be non-significant and read as 'no differences', reaching the issue's conclusion by a binary-outcome null.

decision: Hatred needs perceived stakes: teams that took a prize from you get hated, so nobody hates the Rockies.
anova_analysis: t-test of hate sentiment, teams with recent titles/blocking vs not
why: The issue makes no formal inference, and a crude title vs no-title comparison would point the same way.

decision: The single January window left about 1,200 portal players with nowhere to go and raises roster variance.
anova_analysis: none possible
why: The main finding is a count with no inference to get wrong.

decision: A 7-6 head-to-head record cannot distinguish two teams; the tiebreaker adds noise, not data.
anova_analysis: one-sample t-test of game-win indicator (13 games) against .5
why: The analyst's test returns p near 1 and the same verdict that the tiebreaker cannot separate the clubs.

decision: New York's three teams carry 129 drought years vs Washington's 49; D.C. fans have less misery.
anova_analysis: none possible (3 vs 3 droughts)
why: Pure arithmetic on championship dates, nothing for the tool to change.

decision: 54% is about the Wild Card line itself, so aiming at it gets you in only sometimes; it is a floor, not a target.
anova_analysis: t-test of win% for playoff vs non-playoff teams
why: The tool shows playoff teams win more but cannot state the chance of getting in at 54%.

decision: The worst record bought only a weighted lottery chance; Charlotte missed Anthony Davis.
anova_analysis: none possible (one team, one lottery)
why: The point is the probability a lottery hands the prize to the worst team, which the tool cannot express.

decision: Game 1 winners take the Cup 77% of the time, but a 1-0 lead alone is worth about 66% between even teams; the rest is better teams winning openers.
original_tool: historical base rate plus binomial series math
anova_analysis: t-test of Cup wins, Game 1 winners vs losers
why: The analyst would credit the whole 77% to the Game 1 win, missing that better teams self-select into winning openers.

decision: At Cincinnati winning gets your coach poached, and the program drops the year after each departure.
anova_analysis: paired t-test of win% final coach year vs year after departure (n=5)
why: The issue's reading is descriptive and the analyst's paired test of the drop would say the same.

decision: Conclusions drawn only from survivors mislead; sports arguments must count the non-survivors (e.g., failed tanks).
anova_analysis: t-test comparing outcomes of visible successes (e.g., tank teams that won) vs others
why: An analyst who never asks about design compares only the survivors in the data and commits the exact error the issue warns against.

decision: MLB team records are far more year-to-year predictable than Steamboat snowfall; analog-year matching works for baseball, not snow.
anova_analysis: median split last year's value, t-test of this year's value, MLB and snow separately
why: Significant for MLB and non-significant for snow gives the same verdict, but loses the size comparison and reads snow's null as no memory.

decision: Predictability depends on each domain's own best predictor: NBA last year is strong, La Nina helps some regions and not others.
original_tool: correlation of leave-one-out predictions with outcomes
anova_analysis: one-way ANOVA of snowfall by ENSO state per station; median-split ANOVA for leagues
why: ENSO ANOVA is a reasonable fit, but per-station p-values replace the common correlation scale and weak signals become 'no effect'.

decision: The Texas high-school body holds enforcement authority the NCAA has lost, because its stakes are too small to draw lawyers.
anova_analysis: none possible
why: Case narrative with no statistical inference for the tool to alter.

decision: Caitlin Clark's closest NBA statistical twin is Oscar Robertson, by both Euclidean and Mahalanobis distance on team-share stats.
original_tool: Mahalanobis and Euclidean distance on era-normalized shares
anova_analysis: none possible
why: The tool has no similarity measure and would compare raw stats across eras and leagues as if they were the same ruler.

decision: Hosts reach the semifinals 59% of the time, a strong but fading prior for the U.S.
original_tool: historical base rate as a prior
anova_analysis: t-test of semifinal rate, hosts vs non-hosts; early vs recent hosts
why: The tool can call host advantage significant but cannot state the U.S.'s chance or treat it as a prior.

decision: 1986 was the year no champion repeated, the last time the Mets stood on top.
anova_analysis: none possible
why: A retrospective with no inference.

decision: Only five teams pass both the talent and maturity gates and are real title threats.
original_tool: gated classification on SP+, FPI, blue-chip and returning production
anova_analysis: t-test of SP+ for teams passing the gates vs not
why: A contender board is a ranking and a title forecast, which the tool cannot produce.

decision: NFL franchises regress to their own mean, not the league's; under a shared cap the Jets' mean is about 7 wins.
original_tool: franchise mean win levels over 20 seasons
anova_analysis: one-way ANOVA of season wins by franchise (32 groups)
why: A franchise-factor ANOVA finds the same stable club differences, though it ignores serial dependence.

decision: Fantasy matchups are decided in high-variance positions, not by your best average scorer.
anova_analysis: t-test of mean points by position
why: The tool compares means only and cannot pose where the chance of winning a matchup is decided.

decision: A 71% season team is only about a 52% bet in one sudden-death moment, so the deepest wounds share a shape.
anova_analysis: none possible
why: The decision is the chance of one event, which the tool cannot express.

decision: Notre Dame's $20B endowment can spend about $655M a year, 39% of costs, so the school is not going free.
anova_analysis: none possible
why: Budget arithmetic with no inference.

decision: Flipping a middling team takes about 4 stars in baseball and 1 in basketball (a QB in football).
anova_analysis: one-way ANOVA of team wins by number of stars, per sport
why: Star-count ANOVAs would be significant everywhere but cannot answer the counterfactual of how many swaps move a team.

decision: A top-3 bullpen on a 50-win team had the fewest leads to protect, so selling it was right.
anova_analysis: median split on bullpen ERA, t-test of team win%
why: The analyst would find good bullpens go with winning and say keep it, missing that value depends on leads to protect.

decision: The 2027 Preakness move does not add rest to the series; it shifts the squeeze in front of a longer Belmont.
anova_analysis: none possible
why: Calendar arithmetic with no inference.

decision: A 14-game streak is worth most in midseason (May), less in April, and almost nothing late.
anova_analysis: none possible
why: The value of a streak is a change in playoff probability, which the tool cannot compute.

decision: An 80% make rate from 43 yards is a fact about many kicks, not a property of the one kick that decided Chicago's game.
anova_analysis: t-test of make rate by distance group
why: The tool reports group rates but has no language for the chance of one kick.

decision: The eliminated Athletics can move about 201 points of other clubs' playoff odds; the Mets only 93.
anova_analysis: none possible
why: Leverage is built from simulated playoff probabilities the tool cannot produce.

decision: Out of 1,000 Tommy John pitchers, 791 pitch again but only 735 regain their level; 'success' depends on the finish line.
original_tool: published counts converted per 1,000, review ranges
anova_analysis: one-sample test of return proportion against the quoted 90%
why: An analyst who assumes a measure means the same everywhere takes the 90% at face value and misses the definitional gap.

decision: Returning production does not predict beating the preseason rating; the week-one pattern was noise.
original_tool: correlation and t across 11 seasons, season-by-season stability
anova_analysis: median split on returning-production difference, t-test of rating surprise
why: The pooled t (-1.98) clears .05, so the analyst would call the effect real where the issue judged it too small and unstable to use.

decision: Oregon's 5th-to-76th spread across systems shows a contested ranking; the spread tells you more than the consensus rank.
original_tool: spread of ranks across 35 Massey systems
anova_analysis: one-way ANOVA of rank by team across systems
why: The tool treats each system as an unbiased reading and reports the consensus mean; it cannot pose how contested a single rank is.

decision: Lines land within a point of 50% for every simple rule, but -110 prices add to 104.76%, so bettors lose.
anova_analysis: t-test of cover rate against 50% for each simple betting rule
why: Non-significant tests give 'no edge', the same conclusion, but against the wrong benchmark of 50% rather than the 52.4% break-even.

decision: Pick order in a confidence pool adds nothing to your expected score but nearly doubles your chance to win (22 vs 15 in 100).
anova_analysis: t-test of season score by ordering strategy
why: The analyst finds no mean difference and says order does not matter, missing the doubled chance of winning.

decision: Counted in points the defense looks likelier to jump; in yards per play the gap vanishes, so there is no real offense-defense difference.
original_tool: proportions with intervals, alternative measure, schedule adjustment
anova_analysis: t-test (or two-proportion) of one-SD jump rates, offense vs defense, in points
why: The points-based test would be significant and tell an owner to fix the defense, a finding the better measure erased.

decision: The Cubs banked 126 hope-days and the Mets one; both seasons ended with nothing but felt very different.
anova_analysis: none possible
why: Hope-days are built from forecasts the tool cannot make.

decision: Milwaukee's sweep was not an upset; the better team won and the Dodgers' offense fell short of its own season rate.
original_tool: log5, comparison to own regular-season rates
anova_analysis: t-test of Dodgers runs per game, postseason (8) vs regular season; t-test of team records
why: Small-n tests would be non-significant and read as no change, landing near the issue's caution but by treating a null as absence.

decision: Innings with pitching changes score about five times as many runs because runs cause the change; the new pitcher allows what the situation was worth.
anova_analysis: t-test of runs per inning, innings with vs without a change
why: The raw comparison is hugely significant and says changes backfire, reversing the causal direction the issue found.

decision: A bye is worth about one point against rating, home field three, and almost nothing after a loss.
original_tool: residual vs pregame Elo with rest and home adjustments
anova_analysis: t-test of margin, bye vs normal-week games (13,000+)
why: A huge-n test would call byes significant; same direction, but the analyst reports 'byes help' without the small size or the rating control.

decision: Navy covers big spreads about two times in three but wins outright roughly 1 in 21.
original_tool: betting-market implied probability, historical base rates
anova_analysis: t-test of cover rate, Navy as a big underdog (20) vs other big underdogs
why: The reader's question is Navy's chance to win Saturday, which the tool cannot state.

decision: Only about 9% of traded stars match their past, yet the team that gets the star loses the trade fewer than one time in five.
anova_analysis: paired t-test of star WAR before vs after trade; t-test of WAR received vs sent
why: The analyst gets both numbers' direction but reads the selected-on-peak decline as an effect of the trade.

decision: Assistants of great coaches win 51 vs 46 of 100, but most of that is better programs; the remaining effect is small and may be nothing.
anova_analysis: two-sample t-test of first-job win%, great-boss vs other (203 vs 305)
why: The raw t-test would likely be significant and credit coaching trees with five wins per 100 that mostly belong to the programs inherited.

decision: Two of three AP Top 25 pairs have never met or shared an opponent, so rankings rest on thin direct evidence.
anova_analysis: none possible
why: A count of connections with no inference to get wrong.

decision: The committee ranks small-conference teams about five spots below the formula, but bowl results show the judges were mostly right.
original_tool: rank residuals vs rating formula, bowl-game validation
anova_analysis: paired t-test of committee rank vs formula rank for small-conference teams
why: The analyst treats the formula as the true ruler and declares bias, never checking which measure was wrong.

decision: Five-game streaks add about 1 win in 100 beyond team strength; a hot finish adds nothing to playoff runs once the full season is known.
original_tool: strength-adjusted models across four sports, 200,000+ games
anova_analysis: t-test of next-game win%, teams on 5-game streaks vs not
why: Streaking teams are better teams, so the raw test is significant and says momentum is real.

decision: Under the order's transfer limits an Indiana-style portal rebuild becomes nearly impossible, protecting programs already on top.
anova_analysis: t-test of win improvement, portal-heavy vs HS-first programs
why: The decision is a projection under a new rule, which a comparison of past groups cannot produce.
